activities.anchor: a hypothesis with a vacancy sign
activities.caption: pair each line of drift evidence with what it implied
activities.name: geoWegenerMatch

config.prompt: Wegener's evidence (1912) — pair each observation with the inference it forced:

pairs.left: jigsaw fit of the Atlantic margins
pairs.right: the continents once assembled as one landmass

pairs.left: Mesosaurus and Glossopteris fossils on distant shores
pairs.right: land-dwellers cannot cross an open ocean

pairs.left: the Appalachians continuing into Scotland's Caledonides
pairs.right: one mountain belt, later torn apart by the split
the continents moved through the latitudes

config.why: The evidence floated without a mechanism — he proposed continents ploughing through oceanic crust, and no known force could do that, so the theory was rejected correctly on its own terms.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the geometry, inverted
activities.name: geoPloughSpot

config.prompt: One of these statements of the modern picture is backwards — click it:
lines: Oceanic crust is the top of the moving plate.
It is recycled: created at ridges, destroyed at trenches.
Continents are the low-density, buoyant part that cannot subduct — they ride along.
The seafloor is the fixed sea the continental ships sail on.
Ocean floor is younger than many mountain belts precisely because it is conveyor-belt material.
config.correction: Inverted — the ocean floor is itself the moving conveyor; the continents are the passengers, not the ships.
config.why: Seafloor spreading (Vine–Matthews' magnetic stripes, 1963; ocean crust nowhere older than ~200 Myr) supplied both the evidence and the mechanism.

activities.caption: stack the rheological layers by depth
activities.name: geoRheoOrder

config.prompt: The divisions that matter for the engine — order them by depth:
items: Lithosphere — crust plus the stiff lid; behaves elastically and breaks; ~100 km thick under oceans
Asthenosphere — ~100–350 km; hot, near its melting curve, creeping like glacier ice
Deep mantle — viscosity climbs with pressure
D″ layer — ~2,900 km at the core–mantle boundary; two giant slow provinces
config.why: The real division is rheological, not chemical: rigid rafts above, low resistance beneath — the geophysical division the schoolroom crust–mantle–core picture hides.

activities.caption: file each lava by its tectonic setting
activities.name: geoLavaSort

config.prompt: Melt chemistry is a fingerprint reader — file each product:

items.label: mid-ocean ridge basalt — dry, primitive, remarkably uniform
decompression melting as mantle rises beneath the spreading axis
andesite and rhyolite from water-rich, gas-driven magma
water released from a subducting slab lowering the melting point

config.why: Arc lavas are water-rich and silica-evolved, ridge lavas dry and primitive, plume lavas carry trace-element signatures of deep reservoirs.

config.prompt: GPS geodesy tracks plate interiors to millimetres per year — roughly how fast does the Pacific plate's interior move?
config.why: About 7–10 cm/yr, against the Atlantic's 2–4 — and the GPS reading matches the million-year magnetic-stripe record.
config.context: The faster plates are the ones with long subducting edges — slab pull dominates the balance.

activities.caption: true or false — solid rock, molten myths
activities.name: geoMoltenJudge

statements.s: The mantle is a sea of molten rock on which the plates float.
statements.why: Seismology shows the mantle transmits shear waves — which fluids cannot carry.

statements.s: The asthenosphere is perhaps 0.1–1% melted at most, and flows as a solid.
statements.why: Centimetres per year, by atomic-scale dislocation creep under sustained stress.

statements.s: Only liquids can flow; solid rock cannot.
statements.why: Glacier ice flows too — solids flow when stress is sustained for long enough.

statements.s: The whole force balance — slabs sinking, plumes rising — happens in solid rock.
statements.why: Which is why 'molten layer' pictures make the physics impossible to reason about.

activities.caption: interrogate a hot spot — walk the plume debate
activities.name: geoPlumeBranch

config.root: You are studying an oceanic hot spot. Walk the evidence.

start.text: Tomography under your volcano images a fast conduit reaching the core–mantle boundary.

choices.label: Read it as a deep plume feeding the volcano
choices.feedback: Reasonable — but tomography images conduits under some hot spots and not others, so one case does not settle the plumbing debate.

choices.label: Conclude plumes are unnecessary
choices.feedback: Overreach — a debate needs both sides read; the same tomography supports whole-mantle convection elsewhere.

track.text: The volcanic chain ages linearly to the northwest, with a famous bend 47 million years ago.

choices.label: Read the track as a record of Pacific plate motion over a near-fixed plume
choices.feedback: The standard reading — a 60-million-year record of plate motion; a bend usually records a change in the plate's direction.

choices.label: Read the bend as the plume wandering
choices.feedback: 'Fixed' is measured, not assumed — hot spots do drift relative to each other, but the linear ageing points to the moving plate.

overreach.text: The plume debate stays alive precisely because the evidence is mixed — and plumes remain the engine's second mode, tied to large igneous provinces like the Siberian Traps.

done.text: Hotspot tracks, tomography and the extinction record together: volcanism away from boundaries, on the engine's independent second mode.

drift.text: Plate motion explains the geometry better — the chain is dated, one volcano at a time, across 60 million years.

config.why: Hawaii, Iceland and Yellowstone sit away from boundaries — the plume hypothesis explains them, and the debate over how deep it reaches is measured, not assumed.

activities.anchor: The plate system oscillates on half-billion-year rhythms
activities.caption: sequence one Wilson cycle
activities.name: geoWilsonOrder

config.prompt: The unit of the supercontinent cycle — put it in order:
items: A continent rifts — an ocean opens
Subduction consumes the old, dense floor and the ocean closes
Continents collide — a supercontinent gathers (Pangaea, 335–175 Ma)
The cycle restarts as the assembly rifts again
config.why: Gathering and dispersing supercontinents move weathering, outgassing and ocean gateways — which is why the driving-force question and the habitability question turn out to be the same question.
